<reason>A (CON) built the flashier case: the voluntary-flag-or-attestation-cage fork was a genuinely clarifying device, driven relentlessly from opening to closing, and A's catches (the B1.3-vs-B2.1 "shuffle," "the mandate, renamed," the borrowed-login hole) were real, quotable hits delivered with superior polish and a strong last-word closing. But B (PRO) did more substantive repair work. B answered the fork with a technically credible middle architecture — household-declared minor account, OS withholding unsigned clients and unbounded-feed APIs, store-style conditions — which matches how such controls actually work and defused A's central "bars for everyone" slope, which leaned on an asserted attestation-equals-identity chain and an overstated "sealed lifeline" (recommendation limits don't intercept calls for help). B also tracked the motion's text better: its "app bypass" framing exposed that A's friend's-phone and teen-circumvention lines set a standard no parental rule could meet, and its "capture by design" reframe flipped A's autonomy ground in ordinary homes while the responsibility-lockstep principle gave a clean voting reason. B's costs: a clipped Rebuttal 2 and no direct patch for the borrowed-login point. Net: A wounded B more often; B's route to victory survived more intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.2's "shuffle" catch — B1.3 says a skippable age gate is "no rule," yet B2.1's managed account is a flag apps need not honor — was the most damaging single hit; B4.1–4.2's repair (enforcement lives in the OS withholding what non-compliant apps need, with the household as verifier, not app honor and not state attestation) was the most consequential answer, substantially neutralizing the fork A staked the debate on.</best_rebuttal>
